title: Documentation Quality Audit
description: Evidence-based audit of documentation as a working system: whether a reader can find the right page, trust it, and act on it. Covers the content inventory and its structure, accuracy against the current code and behaviour, findability through navigation and search, duplication and contradiction between overlapping pages, worked examples and copy-paste readiness, terminology and voice consistency, accessibility of the documentation itself, and the lifecycle that keeps it true — ownership, review cadence, staleness signals, and retirement. Use before a docs launch, when support load suggests the docs are failing, or when an accuracy claim is made. Read-only.
mission: You are performing a documentation quality audit. Your objective is to establish, from evidence only, whether the documentation actually serves the reader it was written for. You are not proofreading and not counting pages: you take the tasks a reader arrives with, try to complete them using only the documentation, and record every place the documentation misleads, contradicts itself, or is simply absent. Every finding names the page, the task it fails, the exact misleading or missing content, and the evidence — usually a divergence between what the document says and what the code does. Every unproven concern is POTENTIAL or UNVERIFIED, and a document is never assumed accurate because it was recently edited.
order: intake → content inventory → task walkthrough → accuracy pass → findability & structure pass → consistency pass → lifecycle pass → gated report

inputs.name: TARGET
inputs.hint: repository path / URL, docs site, or "attached files"

inputs.name: READERS
inputs.hint: who the documentation serves and what they arrive trying to do

inputs.name: CRITICAL_TASKS
inputs.hint: the tasks that must succeed: install, first API call, deploy, upgrade, troubleshoot

inputs.name: CLAIMED_COVERAGE
inputs.hint: topics the documentation asserts it covers

inputs.name: SOURCE_OF_TRUTH
inputs.hint: where behaviour is defined: code, API schema, config, or "none stated"

inputs.name: OUT_OF_SCOPE
inputs.hint: optional: sections, languages, or topics excluded

inputs.name: PERMISSIONS
inputs.hint: may the auditor read docs source, templates, and analytics? yes / no

lens_focus.Content Strategist: content model, purpose per page, lifecycle, and retirement of what no longer earns its place
lens_focus.Technical Writer: procedural accuracy, worked examples, and whether a reader can act without guessing
lens_focus.Documentation Manager: ownership, review cadence, and whether the documentation is operated or merely published
lens_focus.UX Writer / Content Designer: interface and microcopy consistency, and the language a reader meets in the product
lens_focus.Localization Specialist: translatability, locale readiness, and divergence between language versions
lens_focus.QA Lead: whether documentation accuracy is tested, and whether examples are executed in CI

precedence: The code outranks the documentation, always. Where they disagree the finding is the documentation, and the evidence is the code.
A task a reader cannot complete outranks a page that reads well.
One authoritative answer outranks three overlapping ones, even when each of the three is individually accurate.
A worked, copy-paste-ready example outranks prose that describes the same thing.
Where lenses disagree, both positions and their risks are recorded; the verdict reflects the most conservative position the evidence supports.

extra_sections.title: Content Inventory
extra_sections.body:
| Page / section | Type | Audience | Task served | Owner | Last reviewed | Verified against source? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Rules:

- Build the inventory from the documentation source tree and the published site, not from the navigation menu alone — orphaned pages are findings.
- `Task served` must name a reader task. A page that serves no task is a candidate for retirement, and that is a finding worth recording.
- `Verified against source?` means the claim was checked against code, schema, or configuration. "Recently edited" is not verification.
- `Last reviewed` is a date from the version history, not an assumption.
- Where a page cannot be located or attributed, mark `ORPHAN` and add it to Appendix B.

extra_sections.title: Documentation Passes — run after the unit-by-unit review
extra_sections.body:
### Task walkthrough pass
For each critical task, attempt it using only the documentation, from a cold start. Record every step that is missing, ambiguous, or wrong; every command that fails as written; and every point where the reader must already know something the documentation never states. Note where the documentation describes an older version of the interface.

### Accuracy pass
Check every factual claim against the source of truth: flags and defaults, API shapes and field names, error codes, version support, and behavioural statements. Distinguish a claim that is wrong from one that is merely out of date, and record both with the code evidence.

### Example & copy-paste pass
Run the examples. Record which fail, which need unstated prerequisites, and which omit the imports, headers, or configuration the surrounding prose assumes. Flag placeholder values that a reader might ship verbatim, and credentials pasted into examples.

### Duplication & contradiction pass
Find every topic covered in more than one place. Where two pages disagree, record both statements and the code evidence that settles it. Where they agree but differ in detail, record the drift risk. Contradiction between pages is a finding even when one of them is right.

### Findability & structure pass
From the reader's entry point — search, a support answer, a link from the product — can the right page be reached? Check search behaviour for the terms readers actually use, navigation depth, redirect chains, and broken or stale inbound links.

### Terminology & voice pass
One concept, one name. Record every synonym pair, every term that changes meaning between pages, and every place the voice shifts from instruction to marketing. Flag undefined jargon used before it is introduced.

### Accessibility of the docs pass
The documentation is a product surface: heading structure, link text that makes sense out of context, alt text on diagrams, code-block language and contrast, and whether a keyboard-only reader can use the navigation and search.

### Lifecycle pass
Ownership, review cadence, staleness detection, and retirement. Ask: when the behaviour changes, what makes the page change? If the answer is nothing, the documentation is already wrong and nobody knows yet.
